speechtext: Annual Report of the Department of Customs and Inland Revenue for the year ended March 31, 1919; Shipping Report of the Department of Customs, containing statements of navigation and shipping of the Dominion of Canada for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1919.-Hon. Mr. Burrell.
On the Orders of the Day:

I should like to ask the acting Prime Minister if there is any truth in the report that the Hon. Albert Sevigny is to replace Mr. DeCelles as Librarian of this Parliament, and if it is true that Mr. DeCelles has asked for superannuation?
No official action has been taken in regard to the matter of which my hon. friend speaks.
On the Orders of the Day:

Has the acting Prime Minister received any further correspondence in connection with the resignation of Judge Robson from the Board of Commerce or bearing on that resignation. If so, may I ask whether the correspondence will be laid on the Table, and when?

I
have received letters, but I am not prepared to say just now what will be brought down.
On the Orders of the Day:

The day before yesterday we were led to expect and hope that a statement would be made to the House regarding the condition of the health of the Prime Minister and his proposed plans. The two members of the Government who went down to New York to meet the Prime Minister have been back for two days now, and the statement which we were looking for with some anxiety is not forthcoming. May I ask whether the acting Prime Minister or some of his colleagues would to-day be in a position to inform the House on this matter?

I
could have given my hon. friend the information yesterday or the day before if he had asked for it. I was waiting to give some hon. member opposite, an opportunity to put the question. With reference to the health of the Prime Minister, I may say that for the two months that he has been away, the improvement in his health has been marked; and if the same rate of improvement continues as I hope it will,-and . I have no reason to fear otherwise-we may expect to have him with us, I think, within two months time.
On the Orders of the Day:

May I ask the acting Prime Minister whether the Imperial Conference which it was expected last session was to be summoned this year, is going to take place, and whether there is any truth in the report that it is likely to be held in Ottawa?

It
is not definitely known, and up to the present it has not been definitely decided that the Imperial Conference will take place this year. I think I may say that Canada, the city of Ottawa in particular, and all our hon. friends on both sides, would be glad if that Conference could be held here. Canada will not put any obstacle in the way of that; in fact she will be very favourable to it.

Consideration of the motion of Mr. Hume Cronyn for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at

the opening of the session, and the proposed amendment of the Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King thereto, resumed from Wednesday, March 3.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak this afternoon, I wish to join with those who have already conveyed their felicitations to the mover and the seconder of the Address in reply to the speech from the Throne. Mention was made by one of the previous speakers to these gentlemen as " props beneath a crumbling edifice." I had rather thought of them as gentlemen who were pillars in the commercial, social, and political life of their country and in their country's Parliament, pillars that were not alone supporting these objects and institutions worthily, but endeavouring worthily to support a Government which, much as fancy and imagination on the part of some might otherwise desire, seems as yet to give no evidence of old age, senility or decay. I do not believe that they are fragile or failing props. They are stalwart supporters of a well based representation of a people's wish and thought in connection with the affairs of this country. There was also to be noted in their speeches a freedom not to criticise the Government, but to express their own personal views, and in so doing, they have simply carried out the practice of the supporters of this Government during the last two years. It is not necessary to have a dead level of monotonous agreement in [DOT]order to have unity and strength. It is quite possible to have variety, difference of view-point, and yet to remain united on the great central and fundamental things. One hardly dare venture further to express -appreciation of this Chamber in which we are gathered. I can only express the hope that its lines and lighting, its colouring and solidity, and the combination of strength and beauty which characterize this Chamber will more than ever characterize the Canadian people collectively and individually.
I must confess my great surprise at the amendment, though it may not be necessary at this stage to assign reasons for voting against it. One can have great regard for the earnest and able address of the leader of the Oppositnon (Mr. Mackenzie King) in moving the amendment, and yet perhaps because of that find it all the more difficult to understand the why, and the how and the what for. For it is known to not a few hon. gentlemen who have gathered here in the last week since the *opening of Parliament that prominent sup-81
porters of his have of their own accord come to hon. members on this side of the House and said, " If any such nonsense is introduced by any of our men as to its being the duty of the Government to make an appeal to the electorate, take no stock in it. It is all bunk." This would seem to be evidence of a lack of unanimity of feeling among hon. gentlemen opposite or else of the failure of some of them to understand the mind of their leader.
In connection with the criticism of the speech from the Throne as altogether inadequately disclosing to (Parliament (the plans of the Government I should like to urge a word of dissent as well as of surprise in view of the references, prolonged and emphatic, to the War-time Elections Act, to the crumbling of representative government, or the ignoring of its principles', and m view also of the criticism of the promise in the speech from the Throne of a new franchise Act. Perhaps the greatest cause for surprise, in my case at least, was the "reference to the Government as being infinitely more concerned With external affairs than with the home business of this country. I am reminded that in different words, but in somewhat the same spirit and with the same point of view, similar statements were made for the first time in my hearing a little over two years ago during a. very vigorous campaign. Canada, as I shall try to show in a moment, has embarked upon world affairs, and can never consent to remain an isolated colony or nation on the northern half of this continent. Before referring to this a little more extendedly, I must express surprise also that there should seem to be drawn from the splendid edifice in which we find ourselves meeting, and from the way in which it has risen to its present almost completed form, a suggestion and symbolism of what the minds of men can do if they are set upon the great task of building well their country and their country's life, for I remember that in the early stages of the reconstruction of this building there were a great many who did not know what the Joint Committee was doing, and what the Government, the Department of Public Works, the architects and the contractors were doing, and consequently there was criticism right and left day after day and month after month, and yet all the time the work was going on. I take it, Mr. Speaker, that any government which is busying itself at any time in the nation's history with matters of vital importance will be so occupied and absorbed-that it

will be impossible for it to explain sufficiently and to the satisfaction of all the facu that it is engaged in a great building or re-building piece of business. The work of reconstruction has been going on in our country, and I think time will show more fully that while ministers of the Crown have not been going up and down throughout the land announcing in strident tones their achievements and accomplishments, nevertheless they have been making a good record as stewards of the people.
I should like to urge that in spite of the difference of opinion in the minds of some of the members of this House as to the importance of having a new franchise Act there are at least two reasons why it is time for such an Act. In the first place we all know that there will be, or should be, a Dominion census next year. [DOT] The people of Western Canada, no matter what their views on the problems that divide us, believe that when that census is taken they can rightfully claim a larger representation in the Parliament of Canada. I do not suppose that western members of tne Agrarian party or of the Liberal party, although they are somewhat hard to find from the West, or of the Unionist group, can be expected to favour an early election in view of the fact that we should have something to show as evidence of the growth of our Western provinces, and that evidence we shall have at the conclusion of the next Dominion census. I have something else in mind, Mr. 'Speaker. There is need for a well-based and adequate franchise Act upon the Statute Books of Canada, as the outgrowth of a conception of citizenship which is to be broader and better-based than anything we have ever had. 1 am of the opinion that no franchise Act that can be brought down will be adequate unless it provides that only those who know enough and feel enough, and those who will to act enough at all times in the nation's history, but especially in time of stress and crisis, shall be given the standing of citizenship. If we have within our borders those who do not measure up to this standard, then let this Parliament demand of the present Government that there shall be conducted that kind of campaign of education in the interests of true Canadianism that will ensure that all who might oppose the view I have just enunciated will find that every person whom they originally might have desired to see included will be so qualified that, in accordance with the principle I have laid down, they will have the right to vote, and not otherwise.

Citizens, Sir, are not merely human beings living within the confines of a country; they are people who have certain attitudes and cherish attachments not merely to the material things of their land, but to that great undefinable something which is not comprehended within the laws and institutions and the customs of a people, and which perhaps can best be described as the national sentiment, or the national spirit. It is for all such, and none other, that the new Franchise Bill, when it is passed by this Parliament, should make provision. If it observes this principle it will prove adequate and will go far towards the building up of a real and sterling national character and national prosperity as well.
With regard to Canada's relation to external affairs, I am sure that even the dreamiest idealist who ever succeeded in getting into any parliament would believe in a country's representatives planning for the development of its natural resources, and giving their time and attention to the affairs of their country. But I am satisfied, from the remarks of hon. gentlemen opposite, as well from those who have spoken on your right, Mr. Speaker, that there is an increasing conviction in the minds of representative Canadians that this does not embrace the whole conception of national life, and that a country's business has become a larger matter in recent years than it used to be. The world was a very big place when even those of us who are young to-day were boys. But the world is a neighbourhood at the present time, and if it is to be a neighbourhood not only commercially and socially, but in the truest economic and international sense, then surely a new country like Canada should not be the last to recognize its part and its place in relation to external affairs.
il desire to read two or three sentences from Sir William Goode's report on economic conditions in Central Europe as presented to the Secretary for Foreign Affairs in the month of January; for I am satisfied that we in Canada who sent so many representatives to the war have never fully realized, since the armistice was signed, what the results have been across the seas. Sir William Goode, among many other pointed statements, writes in these words:
In an endeavour to portray the economic chaos of central and eastern Europe one is apt to take it for granted that the world realizes the human suffering which inevitably follows in its wake. It is a horizon of so much suffering en masse that even those engaged in the work of relief may only be recalled to the individuality of it by a tug at

one's overcoat in the enow-covered streets of Vienna from some mirab child begging for the food which is not there, or by a glimpse into the typhus stricken villages behind the lines where the Poles are still fighting Bolshevik Russia. Vienna, perhaps more than any city In Europe, visualizes the misery that arises from want of food and coal and from the cumulative effects of over four years of ruinous war. Here, In a city of 2J million inhabitants, the sharp contrasts between pre-war prosperity and present day insolvency, between the nervous rich and the starving poor, between the relics of ill-fated monarchy and a revolutionary, but rather desperate, government, stand out with brutal appeal to the imagination.
Concerning Poland he states:
It is estimated that 500,000 tons of cereals must be imported in the year ending September, 1920, to supply the deficit of food in Congress Poland and the provinces of the east and the larger towns, and also to provide seed.
Concerning Czecho-Slovakia he states:
Imports of cereals are needed1 before the next harvest to the extent of 350,000 tons, together with about 400,000 tons of potatoes. The latter can be obtained from Poland. Large quantities of raw materials are required, including wool, cotton, jute, leather, copper, tin, nickel, oilseeds, oils, chemicals, nitrates, and other fertilizers. Czecho-Slovakia is short of locomotives, wagons and materials for repairs' to rolling stock.
Not only does Sir William Goode speak in these terms, but in the "Hearings before the Committee on Ways and Means in the House of Representatives," under date January 10, 1920, I find confirmation and support of his views:
According to the best information obtainable the minimum grain requirement necessary to carry Poland until the next harvest, and which can not be filled anywhere but in the United States, is 300,000 tons. This deficiency is due to a partial failure of the wheat crop and to a lack of fuel for threshing. Poland is at present living under a hand-to-mouth regime.. .
In Austria the acute misery and suffering are probably greater than in Poland. Two-tenths only of the present Austrian State are self-supporting in food, and the remaining eight-tenths, even before the war, produced food to supply themselves for six months of the year at most, and were dependent for the remaining six months upon importations. Consequently, the situation to-day, especially in Vienna, has become exceedingly grave, due to a shortage of coal and food. . . .
What the effect of a general social breakdown in Austria would be can of course only be conjectured.
If time permitted I could quote from several different statements made by Mr. Hoover but one or two brief sentences will suffice:
Poland presents one of the most appalling and appealing situations in Europe. . . . The Austrian situation is the worst in Europe.
He estimates the coming crops in Central Europe as follows:	Poland 75 or 80
per cent of pre-war normal; Southern Russia 80 per cent; Czecho-Slovakia 75 per cent; and Hungary 85 per cent. If Canada is to secure in a permanent way what has been won by her soldiers and others in the war, Canada must continue not only to have a theoretical and seminar sort of interest in Europe but a practical and political interest. If the members of the Government, who to-day should be specially charged with such matters, are not interested, then we who sit behind them, or in front of them, should see to it that they become sufficiently interested to rightly express the feeling and thought of the Canadian people who gave more than half a million of their sons to win the world war. I believe the Government, as those charged with responsibility, have been giving attention to these matters and that they will continue to give them such attention as Canadian sentiment demands.
Britain and the United States have done much to relieve distress. Canada has done something. Why should not Canada do more? Why should there not be an Anglo-American organization functioning to carry on and complete the kind of work that has already been well begun and in connection with such an organization? Why should not Canada have her own inter-related, and yet independent, part to play?
The Argentine has already passed a Bill to this end. Has the Argentine the same stake in the European situation that Canada has? Sir William Goode, in a later part of this same report, as the British director of relief for Central Europe, has referred directly and definitely to Canada. He says:
Invaluable advice was received from the premiers and representatives of the Dominions at the Peace Conference in Paris, particularly from Dr. J. W. Robertson,	who, on
the unanimous invitation of QMr. Hoover and his allied colleagues, attended the meetings of the Relief Section on behalf of the Canadian Government.
If Canada is to follow up and conserve what has already been gained in the way of an increasingly definite status, if Canada is to follow up and make secure that fuller and truer recognition of her nationality and increasing importance in the life of the world, let her not for one moment be so busily concerned in minding her own business that she forgets the business of other countries and so forgets her own.
I want, in resuming my seat, to put in-a brief plea for a broader Canadianism, a harmonious, a united and a not merely tolerant relationship. Tolerance never exists as between friends, much less as be-

tween members of the same family. I want to make a plea for a united life and purpose that will be so broad based that Canada, as her views of democracy and representative government develop-develop at least in their interpretation and application -will recognize some things which were neither recognized nor in existence at the time of Confederation. I believe that a long step in this direction will be taken if we have the right kind of a franchise Act put into effect within the next year.
Then, too, I would like to say, and I am sure we will all agree with it, that in our efforts to legislate, to govern and to develop our own resources and our own life, we will desire and plan so to do these things by co-operation with the other members of the Empire and the other nations of the great wide world.
It is to be hoped that many of the funerals that take place during the next few years will be the funerals of the little Canadians. There are many types. There is the pure MacKay provincial little Canadian; there is the antique colonial; there is the narrow nationalistic Canadian and he may speak more than one tongue. He may have been born to speak the tongue that I am speaking now. There may be the high sounding Imperialist who is a little Canadian, there may be the insular, stay-at-home-on-the-northern-half-of-this-North-American-contin-ent, and let-the-good-old-wealthy-British-mother-pay-the-bills type of Canadian. May these little Canadians rapidly-or as rapidly as a kind Providence sees best-pass off the stage and make room for their nobler and broader chested successors who will see a Canada which actually extends from the Atlantic to the Pacific and which has fair measurements north and south. Canada has moved out too far into the world and the world's affairs ever to be satisfied to retrace her steps. Her status in the Empire and in the League of Nations has been established, though definitions may be made more perfect in the coming years. We cannot go back upon what we have gained and what we have established. While our duty remains here on the northern half of this, the greatest continent in the world, our destiny will be linked up with the great brotherhood of the nations and external affairs will mean more to us in each succeeding year as we continue to take care in a large way of the growing, and increasingly important, business of this our Canadian country.
Mr. THOMAS W. CALDWELL (Victoria and Carleton): Mr. Speaker, after having

listened to so many eloquent and able speeches in the last few days, it is with a certain amount of trepidation that I rise at this time to address the House. That-feeling is all the more marked because I am the first member of the group of hon. gentlemen located on what is styled " the cross benches '' to break the ice at this session, and judging by the remarks of some of the speakers who have preceded me the water will be fairly cold. The impression seems to exist among some hon. members of this House, especially among those sitting on the Government side, that the independent group in this House are here to represent solely the farmers. I would like to correct that impression and to warn hon. gentlemen who entertain such an opinion that while our numbers, as yet, in this Chamber are but few, I believe we represent a majority of the public of Canada to-day. I believe that fact is realized by the hon. gentlemen to whom I refer, and that if it were not for it they would not be quite so concerned about our appearance in this Parliament. It is not our " contemptible little army " they are worrying about; they are apprehensive of the public opinion they must meet at the next general election.
Regarding the amendment before the House, I believe that if the electors of Canada were asked to pronounce upon it they would support it by an overwhelming majority. They would do that not -because it was moved., by the leader of the Liberal Party or because it is a liberal motion at all. In the first place the Union Government was formed to carry on the war, and its term of office was to be during the war and until demobilization was completed. The Union Administration was also to be composed of fifty per cent Liberals and fifty per cent Conservatives. I may say that I was a supporter of the Union Government at that time and on those terms. Now the war has ended, demobilization has been completed, and it looks to me, Mr. Speaker, as if the Union Government was done, too, as a Union Government, because nearly all the Liberal members of the Union Cabinet have resigned, giving as their reason for so doing that they believed the term for which the Union Government was elected had expired.
In the next place, I do not feel that this Government has been consistent in its policy. It has preached greater production, and has not enacted legislation to encourage production; and although it promised to appoint a committee to prepare tariff legislation to be brought before

the House at this session, we have no intimation in the speech from the Throne that this will be done. In fact, the inspired press of the Government has stated that no tariff legislation would be brought down this session.
Some of the greatest economists in the world to-day claim that the most important factor in restoring the world to normal conditions is " Production and Economy," and I believe we will all agree with that statement. As I have said, the' present Government has preached greater production but has not passed tariff legislation that would have that result, especially in regard to the necessaries of life. As for economy, I never heard the present Government accused of that. At the time the war was in progress, the Government instituted a campaign for the greater production of food, which was very necessary at that time, and is even just as imperative at the present moment. One would have expected that at a time when the food shortage was so acute the Government would have reduced the duty on fertilizers, which are so necessary, especially to the potato growers of the Maritime Provinces, if the yield was to be increased, and that it would also have lowered the duty on machinery, a very necessary step for the farmers to accomplish greater production, more particularly in view of the very great scarcity of labour. Instead of doing that the Government placed a seven and-a-half per cent war tax on machinery. Thus while the Government preached production, its own policy has been to penalize production.
But your High Protectionist will say " How will you raise the revenue?" While nobody would deny that the customs duty produces some revenue, I believe it is the most extravagant method on earth of raising a revenue.
Take fertilizers, of which we use large quantities in New Brunswick. I speak particularly of conditions in that province because it is that part of Canada I know most about. As I have already said, large quantities of commercial fertilizers are used in Newf Brunswick; they are devoted to the growing of potatoes, which is a staple crop in that province. The duty on mixed fertilizers, Mr. Speaker, is, as you know, ten per cent; and while the Canadian manufacturers of fertilizers import the raw material, or the chemicals, practically free of duty, they appraise against it the cost of the materials and the cost of mixing-manufacturing as they call it-plus the amount of the duty-and charge us the
net result. The result is that you can buy a car of American mixed fertilizers, bring it into any part of Canada and pay the ten per cent duty, at as cheap a rate as it would cost for the purchase of the Canadian mixed material. There are a large number of so-called Canadian fertilizer companies that are merely branches of American companies. These concerns are therefore in the position of charging the consumers of fertilizers in this country with this ten per cent duty. That duty really does not reach our revenue at all; it does not even stay in Canada, it goes to swell the banking account of the American companies.
There are also a number of machinery firms in Canada which are merely branches of American concerns. In some cases they have factories in Canada but in other cases they have not; they merely have assembling plants where the partly manufactured American parts are assembled and put on the Canadian market. These firms also collect the duties on their machinery from the Canadian consumer and the same result happens; it does not go into the revenue of Canada; it does not even stay in Canada, it goes to swell the American bank account. In this way it is manifest that .many thousands of dollars are lost to the revenue of Canada.
Now take the Ford car, which is the poor man's car. In singling out the Ford car I have no criticism of it to make; I have a Ford car which is pretty well worn out but it has given me excellent service. What I have said in reference to the Canadian mixed fertilizers and the Canadian assembled machinery applies perhaps more forcibly to the cheap Canadian made car, especially that type produced by American firms. This year in New Brunswick we are paying for Ford cars $240 more than our American neighbours just beyond the boundary line. Take the case of two men living on each side of the International boundary:	The American pays only $660
for his car while the Canadian has to pay $900 for exactly the same car manufactured by the same firm. The Canadian car is assembled and put together in this country and sold as a Canadian car but it does not pay any duty into the revenue of the country-that goes to swell the American bank account.
Mr. Speaker, the party to which I have the honour to belong has no desire tf>
" submarine the tariff." I believe that was the term applied with respect to our policy by a Cabinet minister speaking in

Montreal a few days ago. We all know that the minister in question (Mr. Meighen) is very apt at phrase making and forming expressions that attract the public ear. But we have no desire to submarine the tariff or anything else. The features of the tariff that we object to are those to which I have made allusion and which permit the Canadian consumer to be robbed without any benefit to the country. These features of the tariff in their operation work exactly the same to-day as the adverse exchange on Canadian money. No doubt the Canadian manufacturer will hail this adverse exchange as a Godsenci to Canada, for it will effectually shut out American competition. It works exactly the same way as the items in the protective tariff, to which I have alluded. If you buy American made goods there is a discount on your money of nearly as much as the tariff will amount to-not as much as it would amount to on a Ford car, more than it would amount to on a mower, and as much as it would amount to on some other farm machinery.
Your high protectionist will say, "Oh, yes, it is just as I thought. Your plea is all for the farmers. You want free entry for fertilizers, farm machinery and the cheap car that the farmers use." And perhaps some people will say, "What does the farmer need with a car?" Mr. Speaker, in this day of high wages and scarcity of labour the farmer in the back concessions needs a car more than his city brother does. It is an absolute necessity when he has to leave his work to go on any errand of business for him to be back home as soon as possible. The old-fashioned method of locomotion by foot or by horseback or by horse and buggy is too slow for this day and generation. So it is absolutely necessary as a matter of economy that the farmer should own a cheap car.
On the other hand, if the duty on farm machinery and on fertilizers increases the cost of production of farm produce more than it should, does it hurt the farmer alone? I claim that it does not. If on account of this high rate of duty on his machinery and the raw material that goes into the production of his crop it costs the farmer more than it should to produce that crop, who suffers most? I claim that the farmer is not the principal sufferer, because perhaps he does not use five per cent of the crops that he produces on his farm. The labouring man, the city man-even I imagine my good friend the member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) uses some of
(Mr. Caldwell.]
the products of the farm. Of course, I do not suppose he would lose as much on the farm produce he uses as he would gain, say, by the duty on ploughs-and he manufactures good ploughs, too, I can assure you; 1 have used them-but I believe that this very feature of the tariff is a big factor in the present high cost of living and the unrest to which it gives rise. I believe that the high cost of living could be materially lowered by making the very changes I have just spoken of.
And here, Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer to the letter that the right hon. the leader of the Government (Sir George Foster) placed on the Table on the 2nd of March-the letter from the Hon. H. A. Robson, K.C., Chairman of the Board of Commerce, as I think that perhaps a paragraph or two from it will corroborate the statement I have made, that the present Government or the past Government-I do not know which you would call it; perhaps it is not past yet. [DOT]
It will be in a little while.

The statement I made was that their legislation has not been favourable to production. Mr. Robson writes:
Dealing with it as a measure to repress profiteering, I have further objection to the Pair Prices part of The Combines and Fair Prices Act (which is the important part of that Act) in that it picks out for profit regulation those classes of producers and traders who deal in the necessaries of life. This regulation does not apply to the great number of other branches of business and occupations. We restrain and discourage the citizen who supplies food and clothing but leave free to profiteer as he pleases the man who deals in nonessentials or luxuries. We do not touch any excessive charging for service involving mechanical or professional experience. There can only be one effect, i.e., to discourage persons from entering into the production and distribution of the necessaries of life.
There is, to my mind, further objectionable discrimination in that the measures for controlling the selling prices of the retailer are in terms fairly effective, while those for reaching the manufacturer are not so.
A profiteering measure to reach the distributing class should, in my opinion, be local in its character and be administered locally. Federal machinery cannot reach the grievance effectually throughout all Canada.
It seems to me further that the Act actually contains a provision which removes the last chance the consumer had to do anything for himself in reducing the cost of living. There never was before the Act anything to prevent a group of consumers from co-operating in the purchase of necessaries. They took their chance of being able to buy. But a declaration of parliamentary policy crept into the Act, and a manufacturer or wholesaler is not bound to

sell to classes who were not accustomed to purchase from such manufacturers and wholesalers. This was designed to head off cooperative movements, which were likely to make progress for the benefit of consumer members and, as I say, restricted a remedy which elsewhere has been of some effect in price control.
If the remarks I have made need any proof, Mr. Speaker, I think you have it there in what Mr. Eobson states, and you have it on the authority of a man in whom the Government had such great confidence that it put him in control of the Board of Commerce.
I do not wish to take up very much of the time of the House, Mr. Speaker, because I find as I travel through
4 p.m. the country that the people believe Parliament wastes too much time in discussion on the reply to the speech from the Throne. But before I sit down I wish to assure the Government of my appreciation of the honour they conferred upon me in my recent election by sending three of their ablest cabinet ministers all the way down to New Brunswick to help my opponent to lose his deposit, especially at a time when Parliament was in session and such very important matters were before it for consideration. I believe that one of those ministers, the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) could hardly be reconciled to the statement which I made at that time that I considered that this visit or visitation of these cabinet ministers to my constituency increased my majority by at least one thousand votes.
Well, Sir, I will try to enlighten him. I was nominated and ran as an Independent candidate, pledged to support any measure which I believed was for the best interest of Canada, irrespective of which party should introduce it. So that this very decided opposition of the Government to my election seemed to the electors of my constituency to be an admission by the Government that they did not intend to introduce any legislation that would be in the best interests of the people, and my electors resented it. Some of the electors were even mean enough to say that this assistance to my late opponent was for -services rendered in the last general election.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to correct the false impression, which, as 'I have said before, some hon. members seemed to have or were trying to have: That the Independent party in this House is here to submarine the fiscal policy of Canada in the interests of the farmers, regardless of all other industries or people in this Dominion.
I wish to assure this House, so far as in me lies, that we are here not to tear down, but to give what assistance we can towards the building up of a Greater Canada, so that not only the people of this Dominion but the people of the whole world may say, "Surely Canada is a bit of God's own country."
Mr. WILLIAM A. BUCHANAN (Lethbridge) : Mr. Speaker, I will be quite frank at the outset and say the remarks I am about to make are not inspired so much by the speech from the Throne as by the amendment offered by the hon. leader of the Opposition. I am in this position that, so far as I am concerned, an election can come at any moment; but at the present time I want to make a choice and in making that choice I desire to consider the interests of the section of the country from which I come, and at the same time I do not want to be sectional in the observations I make though I wish to make them from the standpoint of the western provinces.
The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) has moved an amendment demanding an election. Next year we know that a census is to be taken in this country, following which census there should be a redistribution, and in my judgment, as a result of that census and redistribution, we would have, in the Prairie Provinces, or if you were to take all the western provinces, twenty new members in the House of Commons. If I were to support the amendment of the leader of the Opposition and it carried, what would be the result? There would be an election as there was in 1911, and the West would not obtain, for four or five years to come, its full representation on the census of 1921. If the Government is prepared to state that there will be a census and redistribution next year, I prefer to take chances on the Government of the day rather than to withhold for four or five years the proper representation that the West should have in this House. I know there are represented in this country and in this Parliament of the Dominion of Canada interests which are anxious that the West should not have its full representation until the last possible moment. I do not know whether the leader of the Opposition desires to associate himself with those interests in Eastern Canada; but we know that those people do not want Western Canada to have any larger voice in the affairs in this country than it has at present if they could in any way withhold the representation to which Western Canada is entitled. In the West we feel that

we are entitled to our full representation, and that, if we are to have an election at this time, that representation will be delayed for foui or five years.
May I be personal for a moment and explain my position as a member of this House? 1 do not feel at the present time that I am wedded to the support of the Government of the day. I feel that I have fulfilled my obligations to Union Government, because I was elected as a Liberal supporting Union Government. I advocated Unionism and supported it; I was elected as a supporter of Union Government for the purpose of carrying on the war, and, in my judgment, that period has elapsed. But am I at this moment to precipitate an election and thus prevent the section of the country in which I live from having its proper representation in the Commons of Canada? I prefer to act as a free lance in this House, and to avoid an election if necessary, in order that Western Canada may have, as soon as possible, its full and proper representation in this House. What would happen if we were to defer the question of an election for another year? We have only this choice to make: We have the Opposition and we have the Government; and so far as I am concerned, the toss of a coin would satisfy me in that respect and probably would satisfy a good many people in this country. I am prepared to take a chance on the Government (for another year in order that we should have a census and a redistribution. I believe it would only be necessary to have one session of Parliament following the present session before we could have a redistribution and before an appeal could be made to the country on the basis of a representation in accordance with the census of 1921.
I have no hesitation in saying that 1 believe that Union Government fulfilled the purpose for which it was elected. I have always said so, and I have no apologies to jnake for supporting Union Government. But when we come to times of peace; v'hen we are to discuss domestic problems, then there is bound to be a probability that I shall differ with this Government and that I shall want to align myself with those who agree with the views that I have consistently advocated in times of peace. I am perfectly satisfied with the record of Union Government as a war Government, and I think history will prove that Union Government served the purpose for which it was elected and was a great necessity to Canada in war time. I hope I have

made my position clear on the question of the amendment.
I am not in favour of the amendment if we can have an election next year following the census and a redistribution. I prefer to carry on for the present in order that Western Canada may have its proper representative voice in the affairs of this country. As -I said before, I know there are people and interests who do not want Western Canada to have its proper representation in this Parliament at the present time, I am not prepared to encourage those people in their views; on the contrary I am content to wait for the earliest possible realization of the representation to which Western Canada is entitled.
As I said in rising, my main purpose in speaking this afternoon was to make myself absolutely clear as to my attitude towards the .amendment. While I am on my feet I should like to make some observations regarding what has been called the unrest which exists in this country and how it is best for us, as a people and as a Parliament, believing in the institutions which exist in Canada and which are the foundations of the Government of this country, to act towards this seeming unrest. I know there is a good deal of agitation in the country. There is what might be called revolutionary sentiment in Canada. People are going about spreading new doctrines, and what are we as members of Parliament and as citizens of this Dominion doing to combat that sentiment ? I do not believe in repressive measures, but I do think we should have educational measures to counteract the agitation which certainly exists throughout a good part of the country. We should go out and educate as to our system of Government the new citizens of this Dominion, the people who are being appealed to by thes.e agitators. We should let them understand that they have in this land the fullest freedom and opportunity to realize their ambitions if they can convert the majority of the people to their views. We should do that rather than adopt repressive measures which would make them feel that that kind of freedom does not exist in this country. It must be remembered that I am not in sympathy with the views that are being advocated by those people, but I am expressing my views as to what we should do to combat them in the best way so as to avoid further trouble and to restore amongst those people confidence in our institutions.

Many charges have been made that there is profiteering in this country; and that the control of the Government is in the hands of a few people. If that be the case, it is our duty to remove that control. If it be not the case we should enlighten the people. I happened to read the other day an article in an American paper concerning a district affected by the recent steel strike. One of the causes at the back of that steel strike undoubtedly was this continual talk of profiteering; that the steel corporation and its shareholders were making huge returns from the business and that the employees were not getting their fair share. One steel factory in the state of Ohio, taking its employees into its confidence, had enlightened them as to the business, as to the dividends that were being paid and as to the cost of operation. And as a result those men were satisfied that the industry was paying them all it could afford to pay them under the circumstances so that, when the steel employees throughout the United States were called upon to strike, the men at this particular mill did not go out. I think there is an obvious, lesson there for all the industries of this country, and that is, to enlighten the men who are serving in those industries and to enlighten the people in reference to these charges of profiteering. That can be done quite easily, and it will save a great deal of the industrial unrest that exists, and help to remove a great deal of the suspicion which exists in the minds of the people. I believe that a good many of our industrial troubles in Canada are due to suspicion more than to anything else. The men are suspicious of their employers, and the employers are suspicious of the men identified with their unions, and this feeling of suspicion prevents them getting together. If both sides would only come out in the open and deal frankly with each other, a great many of our industrial difficulties could be avoided.
It has been my custom in this debate to make a declaration of my views on the fiscal policy of the country. I want to say that I stand where I have always stood, in favour of the lowest kind of a tariff. But I would say to the Government and to the House that in regulating the tariff we should aim at relieving the burdens that are imposed upon the mass of the people, and aim also at the development of our natural resources. If we could have had a tariff in this country that would enable all the implements of production that are used in
the development of our resources to be got as cheaply as possible, it would do a great deal for the development of our resources and toward relieving the country of its financial obligations. If the implements that are used in mining, for instance, in lumbering, in fishing, and in agriculture, could be made as cheap as possible to the people who'are producing along those lines, there would be an encouragement to greater production, and the richer the country becomes in production the better position we shall be in to meet our financial obligations. I am not one of those who believe we can go out and slash the tariff all to pieces at the present time. I know that for some years to come we must utilize the tariff for raising revenue. But, the tariff should be directed wholly toward raising revenue, rather than to, protecting certain industries that have enjoyed protection in this country for a great many years. Possibly, members of the Government who are not moving around so much and getting in touch with the minds of the people would like to know what the feeling of the people is with regard to the protected interests. To be frank, the great mass of the people, who are finding it hard to live to-day, and who see everything they buy rising higher and higher in price, realize that the men who are engaged in the protected interests in this country are living in comparative ease and comfort, having amassed a considerable fortune. They say that is due to the high protection given to those industries. Surely if the men engaged in these protected industries have amassed fortunes through a protective tariff, it is time we reduced that tariff and gave the people who are working day in and day out to make an honest living a chance not only to do so, but to save a little. That is the view of the people I come in contact with from day to day. We must have a tariff to raise revenue, but I do not think that tariff should be directed towards the protection of industries that have enjoyed protection in this country for so many years.
I should like to make a suggestion about the income tax. I am an advocate of income tax. I Relieve that if it is properly administered it can be made to yield a great revenue to this country, but I feel (and I do not place the blame on the Minister of Finance) that the tax has not been efficiently administered up to now, and that we are not getting from it the amount of revenue we should. I believe there are people who are evading the tax. I have only recently received communications intimating

that some people are boasting that they have not paid the tax while some of their neighbours paid it. I have not their names or I would be glad to give them, for I have no sympathy with any man who evades paying the taxes imposed in this country. At the same time, I feel the administration has been weak, largely because an attempt has been made to centralize it'instead of spreading out the organization a little more widely in the different provinces. In the province of Alberta, for instance, until quite recently I understand we had only one income tax officer, located in the city of Calgary. Another officer has since been located in Edmonton, but the oflicers must be closer than that to the population of the country, or they cannot reach the people who should pay the income tax. I think there should be officers in all the larger centres of all the provinces. I believe the expense would be repa>id a hundredfold by the intimate knowledge they would have of the people liable to pay this tax.
I should like to make another observation. We have at the present time government ownership of railways on a very extensive scale, and I am glad we have it. I believe that government ownership can be made a success, and the Government of the day should see that every effort is made to encourage the efficient operation of our government roads, but I do hear complaints that some of the roads we have had in our possession for some years are not being operated efficiently-that the roadbeds have not been improved to the necessary extent to make operation successful. As an advocate of government ownership I would urge the Government to use its utmost efforts to get at the head of the Government system the most efficient administrator that can be obtained. We have a big system, bigger than the Canadian Pacific. I do not think the question of salary should be a consideration. We should get the very best railroad man.on this continent at the head of the system and pay him a big salary. That is the only way to make the system a success. Politics should be kept [DOT] entirely out of the operation of the system. So far as I know, politics have not entered into the operation of the railway, but the people generally feel a little doubtful of the success of government operation, and it is up to the Government to prove that government operation can be made a success; if they do, the people will be satisfied.
In closing, I should like to pay a tribute to the attitude that has been taken recently by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. 
Rowell) in connection with the reservations to the Peace Treaty proposed in the United States Senate, which, if adopted, would take away from Canada its place in the League of Nations. I believe that the President of the Privy Council has the bulk of the people behind him in his attitude. I do not want to see Canada participate in any more wars, but I say that the part Canada played in the recent great war in Europe entitles her to a place in the League of Nations, and to a voice in deciding whether or not there shall be wars in the future. I have no desire to cast any reflection on the United States, but I will boast of this fact, that Canada was in the war from its inception, and sacrificed thousands of men for the principles for which they were fighting; and this nation therefore has just as much right to a voice in the councils of the League of Nations as has the United States of America.

Mr. Speaker, I rise with considerable diffidence to make this my maiden speech in the House of Commons, and I trust that hon. gentlemen at the other end of the Chamber will be able to hear me distinctly, because it is my desire that some of the remarks which I intend to make shall reach them. In my new capacity as a member of the House of Commons I have watched with considerable interest the gladiators, as I may perhaps term them, on both sides of the House. I have seen blows offered and parried, and the proceedings, I must say, have at times been rather diverting. As I have listened to the debate I have wondered whether all these charges and counter-charges have been really indispensable to the conduct of the affairs of the Dominion of Canada, or whether they have become necessary as a matter of tradition. Be this as it may, I beg to add my small mead of praise of the sentiments that have already been expressed by so many hon. gentlemen in this House in reference to the admirable addresses that have been delivered by the mover and seconder of the Address in reply to the speech from the Throne. The exalted office discharged by those hon. gentlemen has not fallen to my lot, and my remarks must of necessity be more of a practical kind. Nevertheless I can assure this House that I duly appreciate the lofty ideals and the broad views to which expression was given in both of the addresses in question, and though I may lack a full conception of the height and broadness of vision which should characterize a representative of the people, I hope

to prove that I am absolutely sincere in my appreciation of the views which my hon. friends, the mover and seconder of the Address, have so well stated. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I'was gratified to have the privilege of being present at the opening of Parliament in this beautiful building. As I viewed its imposing magnificence and its beautiful architectural design from the outside; as I have promenaded the corridors; as I have listened to hon. gentlemen describing the beauties of the building, I myself have acquired a deeper conception of true Canadianism than I heretofore had.
I have no doubt that this building is a fitting monument to the greatness of the Canadian people; and to the architect and those associated with him I am constrained to offer my congratulations on the splendid result of their genius. I admire, and indeed almost envy, the mind of the man who has such a large conception of everything that is worthy and inspiring as has been so ably exhibited in the beautiful and spacious building in which we are privileged to be assembled. I am sure that this building will stand out as a prominent landmark among all the public buildings, not only of Canada but of the North American continent, and will be a credit to this newly recognized young giant, the Canadian nation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have not come here in any fighting spirit; I have come in a measure to tender to hon. gentlemen the olive branch. I am temperamentally a man of peace, not essentially disposed to combat; although it has been known in the past, I think, that I can retort when severely attacked. But I do believe, and sincerely so, that the hon. gentlemen who compose this House on both sides will listen with reason, and I trust with more interest than we have seen displayed in the past, to every statement of conditions as they really are. I am inclined to think that when we express our convictions, and place before this House our conception of conditions as they exist in the country to-day, hon. members may be disposed to revise their ideas, and that possibly some of the decisions that have already been arrived at may be reversed. I think that the consensus of opinion in this House inclines to the view that what we shall have to say will be hearkened unto, because whatever stand we may take on any question that may call for consideration in this House will be taken in all sincerity. Naturally my viewpoint, as I address this House, must be taken from western conditions, and I believe that I am in a far better position to know those conditions than many hon. members in this Chamber. I deplore the fact that any inference should be sought to be drawn that the movement with which we are associated-the Agrarian Movement as it is called-is a class movement. Let me assure you, Mr. Speaker, that in its initiation it was not intended to be such, and that fact has been proclaimed on platforms and in the press. Indeed, Sir, we know that it never could succeed as a class movement. The platform of the Canadian Council of Agriculture, called now the new National Policy, is big enough and broad enough to embrace all classes in this Dominion of ours, and to protect the interests of the nation, and if hon. gentlemen refuse to accept this statement as true and insist upon describing us as a class organization, then I can only say that the fault is not with us. For we hold an open hand and are ready to co-operate with all in order to further the interests of Canadian life. This statement is known to be true by those who have had an opportunity of studying our platform at first hand. They know that no distinction has ever been drawn between rural districts and tfrban centres, and an examination of the returns will show that the people who are best conversant with that platform have all approved of it, whether in the urban centres or in the rural districts. That fact should be sufficient to dispel the idea that ours is a class movement, and it should not be necessary for an individual to stand up in this House in order to proclaim it. It has been stated with great insistence on the hustings and elsewhere that in this movement there is an aim to further the interests of a class.
It is a fact that our own conviction was that such an idea could not, and should not, succeed. If hon. gentlemen accept my statement and my interpretation of our attitude, I am sure we will not have the charge thrown at us that we favour class legislation or a class movement. I am proud to be able -to say that that is the feeling of the great farmers' organization of the West, whose platform, as I said before, is big and broad enough for all who may wish to stand upon it and to assist us in our effort to make Canada a better place to live in than it has been in the past.

If I join your organization, not being a farmer, will I be permitted to take any part in determining its policy?
12(1

I am pleased that the hon. gentleman has asked me that question and I will reply in the affirmative. I wish to make this further statement that at the convention which we held-and I believe we held one of the most democratic conventions that ever took place in Canada- there were eighteen names upon the slate, four of them divines, three of them merchants, two (professional men and the rest farmers, and that it took five and a half hours to 'ballot it through. That is a sufficient answer to the hon. gentleman and it is the best evidence that we do not have a class movement. Urban and rural centres both sent their delegates; fourteen hundred men and women sat in that skating rink .and it took them five and a half hours balloting in order to find this unworthy individual. Surely that should be a sufficient answer, surely that should be proof that the words that I have spoken here have been spoken in all sincerity and that there is no basis for the fear that some hon. gentlemen seem to have that this is destined to be a class movement.
Is it not true that in the rural constituencies in Alberta they will allow no one but a farmer to be a member of the organization?

I speak for the province of Saskatchewan alone where I am best known. I am the only representative from the West who has been elected on the platform of the Canadian Council of Agriculture. Consequently, the experiences of Alberta are as yet an unknown quantity-I do not know. While I speak to the House to-day I speak across what may be called No Man's Land for what, as my colleague who preceded me said, may be regarded as the contemptible little army. Perhaps I should not use that expression but if we go 'back to find a precedent for its use on the war-torn fields of Europe we find that the term was made applicable not to the assaulting party but merely to the defensive party. While we take that position here to-day, we hope the day will come, and come quickly, when hon. gentlemen seated in this House will accept our policy and help us. That is our hope and ambition.
My hon. friend who preceded me made reference to the assistance he received during his election down in New Brunswick. I have a somewhat similar tale to tell although the fact is that my opposition did not come from members of the Government. I entertain no animosity towards the hon. .gentlemen who came to my electoral dis-

trict-none whatever; in fact, I believe our friendship has been cemented as a result of their visit. Scripture tells us that wise men invariably come from the east. We were always led to believe that when wise men came from the east they came in bodies of three. It was heralded all over the electoral district of Assiniboia that three were to come. However, when the train pulled into our little station, only two got off. They were dressed immaculately and they carried leather grips, something that was scarcely understood in the west. These hon. gentlemen, a,s they gazed upon the people who were working in the town, were no doubt filled with wonder that these people simply went on about their work although' they were in the heat of a political campaign. Yet it is a fact, to make a long story short, that these gentlemen returned east and I am satisfied that they 'returned wiser than when they came west. I would give a cheque for a hundred dollars of my sessional indemnity to find out swbat actually took place among the three when they again met after the election in Assiniboia. An hon. gentleman on the Government side of the House made reference to the election in Assiniboia and said that the majority was approximately 4,000. Let me inform the hon. gentleman that there was a majority of 5,294 which was amply sufficient to tell the people of the Dominion that the electors of that constituency at any rate believed they had a grievance. It was perfectly expressed by the exponents of our new platform and it is a fact that the people of Canada have become educated. They have become educated along lines of progress which they believe it is necessary for this Dominion to pursue and the people of Assiniboia showed the result of their belief in the action they took on the 27th day of October.
A sentiment was given expression to by an hon. gentleman on the Opposition side of the House to which I wish to make a brief reference. That sentimerit, expressed by an hon. gentleman who stands high in the Liberal party was that he would not trade with any nation that would not recognize our Canadian dollar as being worth one hundred cents. I would direct the attention of the House to the fact that immediately after the American Civil War the American dollar went down in value tc about 37 cents and it i.s not. on record that the Government of Canada refused to take advantage of the difference in exchange in dealing with our neighbours to the south. There must be consistency. If that hon. gentleman lived near the inter-

national boundary in Saskatchewan and Alberta and he found that his neighbour *within a mile or two of him was receiving from 70 cents to $1 a bushel more for his wheat than he was privileged to receive -on this side, I am sure he would take advantage oi every opportunity that, was afforded to take his wheat across the line, receive that extra 70 cents or $1 and bring hack good American money and spend ,t with the merchants in Canada. That is just as loyal, just as true a.s the nositmn which the hon. gentleman takes and it is the proper business attitude. Consequently I do not think the sentimenr. oi not trading with a country that refuses to ajooept our ,money at ipar should carry much weight with the real business men of Canada. I do not suggest this so much in a spirit of criticism as I do from the purely business point of view. Business is business and the best interests of the country require that we should encourage an interchange of commodities across the international boundary rather than that we should place obstructions, sentimental or otherwise, in the way. I visited the town of Sherwood, North Dakota, during our campaign to get direct information on this subject. The operator in one of the elevators there had compiled figures, and he showed them to me, disclosing that $12,000 of good American money on the proportion of wheat that had been brought into that town from the Canadian side-a $12,000 equity-had been paid at that time to Canadian producers who had marketed their wheat there. How near will the price we shall receive for our participation certificates equal the price we feel we should receive. I have a few of those in a little box at home for which I was offered five cents a bushel. That was the valuation some of the business men of Canada placed upon our participation certificates. I refused, of course, to accept the offer; but the fact remains that I would prefer to accept nothing for my participation certificates than take a premium of five cents a bushel. I for one never expect to receive for my participation certificates the same amount that my American cousin on the south side of the line enjoys.
The question has been asked " for what do we stand?" From our viewpoint one of the most important things we stand for is a big reduction in the tariff, a question that was well taken by the hon. gentleman who preceded me. He explained the matter in a manner that well commends
itself to me and I am not now going to discuss at length the protective features of the tariff. I quite understand that later on an opportunity will be given of going into the subject at length. I shall simply now content myself by placing on record the statement that I am utterly opposed to the. high protective principle involved in the tariff and let the matter go at that.
We not only stand for a reduction in the customs duties but we advocate the nationalization of our national resources and various other policies which I will not occupy the time of the House by dwelling upon at the present.
The planks set out in our platform have on many occasions given cause for alarm to many of the " interests " in this country and they have asked in dismay "where will the revenue come from if these policies are carried out?" Some of the planks in our platform have been called destructive, but we have a constructive policy to replace anything that may appear as destructive, a constructive policy Sir that I believe would be in the interests of Canada as a whole. What that policy is can be determined by a close and earnest study of the provisions set out in the planks of our policy.
Does the hon. gentleman believe in the principle of protection at all, whether it be high or low?
I do not.
That is a plain statement.
The grain growers do not want any protection.

I would like to further
add that I never did believe in that policy and I do not expect I ever will.
That is quite explicit.

Now as to the question
of where the revenue is to come from. That has been a very interesting subject of debate during our campaign in the West and where the merits of the question have been discussed the people who have heard our explanations have been thoroughly and perfectly satisfied. Let me give an illustration as to possible sources of revenue. On the Atlantic coast, at Montreal, at Fort William, at Hudson bay, and on the Pacific coast there are great stretches of water frontage which have fallen into the hands of private individuals. Providence created them but through the operation of the institutions and orgariiza-

tions of our country they have been acquired by private individuals. The owners of these frontages through their development have become wealthy. Possibly as low a sum of $100 was paid for some of these privileges and ultimately they were sold for as much as $600,000 for no effort on the part of the individual who received the equity. I maintain and I insist that it is only right and proper in the interests of the people of Canada that the Dominion Government should appropriate ninety per cent of the money that accrued to such speculators and use it for the purpose of administering the national affairs.
We are told by 'scientists that the whole of the province of Alberta and large areas of Saskatchewan are underlined with coal. Up near the Pas in Manitoba we also know that large and valuable deposits of copper occur. I was informed that on one quarter section alone the vein was known to be worth $1,000,000. The profits from these great natural resources are going to the country to the south owing to concessions to American capitalists'. They are taking our heritage. Our birth right and heritage is being handed over to outsiders and yet we are bewailing the fact that we cannot find sufficient revenue to run the country. I have indicated possible sources of revenue to say nothing of other planks in our platform with respect to taxation -not indirect taxation. The policy of direct taxation is something that the people can see and understand. That indirect taxation should have been resorted to means that the people have not understood and do not appreciate the conditions involved. It is a form and system of deception and I think no Government should follow out any such principle. At any rate that is my earnest belief.
I desire now for a few minutes to discuss conditions that pertain to my own electoral district. It is a fact which has already been mentioned here that for three sessions Assiniboia has been unrepresented. Let me qualify that statement, in a measure and at the same time pay my tribute to the hon. gentleman who preceded me in the representation of. the constituency and who has now been elevated to the Senate. I know for a fact that the hon. gentleman in question on many occasions did his best for Assiniboia and succeeded admirably in having that district represented. That however was a form of indirect representation and owing to the extra burdens that have been placed upon the hon. gentleman in question by his elevation to the Senate

the district of Assiniboia has been deprived of the direct representation to which it was entitled. I am not now speaking in criticism of the Government. The time perhaps was not ripe for the great agrarian movement which has since developed such strength to manifest itself had a by-election been brought on earlier. The fact nevertheless remains that Assiniboia has for some time been unrepresented and conditions there have been more or less in a state of chaos. The conditions that have developed there, from an agricultural point of view are deplorable and before I came here I had some correspondence with members of the Government asking that some relief might be afforded to certain of the farmers in south eastern Saskatchewan as a result of repeated droughts, loss of crop, and last year the devastating havoc caused by grasshoppers.
I hold in my hand representations made by six municipalities regarding the deplorable conditions resulting from the devastation caused by grasshoppers last year. I have asked that these settlers, these men that want to produce for the sake of the country, be given an opportunity to retrieve their position. I am told that they are to be given an opportunity-that the Dominion Government iwill back their efforts to purchase seed. iBut what is the use of seed for their horses this winter? These men want money. In 1916 rust and hail destroyed a large portion of their crops. I myself suffered a total loss that year. In 1917, 1918 and 1919 there were partial losses. These men need help-not protection, not for a moment. They want assistance so they can purchase feed for their animals and go ahead and produce 100 per cent. I do not wish to read the letters which I have here corroborating the statements I have made, letters from the reeves and the secretaries of the municipalities affected, hut I would ask you to accept my word that I am truly representing the conditions that obtain in that Western country. I would respectfully ask for recognition of the appeal I make on behalf of those people that they receive greater assistance than has been tendered to them through the medium of the Provincial Governments, and I would like to know that they will receive such assistance very soon, because at this season of the year they are making strenuous efforts to carry on; but under existing conditions, no matter how strenuous each individual effort may be, those people are going to be absolutely incapacitated from producing what they are so anxious to produce-one hun-

dred per cent, a percentage which the country needs and wishes them to produce. '
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, referring once more to the three sessional indemnities due Assiniboia, I would suggest that a requisite amount be added to the total of those indemnities and given to these people to afford them a chance to overcome the adverse conditions which have almost overwhelmed them, for it is a fact that they have suffered much, and I am sure that any help that may be accorded to them they will repay one hundred fold. I have spoken in the interests of my constituents, and I am pleased that you have given me your earnest attention, and, thanking you for your kindness, I will now resume my seat.
