speechtext:
I take this opportunity to say that while there is no disposition on the part of the Chair to restrict debate upon the Address, I would remind hon. members of the subject before the House, and also of the circumstance that there will be a Budget Debate later on in the session.
Mr. WILLIAM F. MACLEAN (South. York): Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity .in making my first address in this very fine Chamber to appeal for a re-5 p.m. turn to parliamentary government, to parliamentary practice, and to parliamentary responsibility for the 'conduct of our public affairs. Partly because of the war no, doubt we departed from parliamentary government and from parliamentary responsibility, but I think the time has come, when an effort should b*e made to return to the former well established principles, and, in the first place, I hold the Unionist Party and the Unionist Government responsible for the maintenance of those principles.
I have alwayfe been a. supporter of Union Government. I pointed out early last session, when opportunity presented itself, that to deal with the war it was necessary to have a union of parties, and that it would be necessary in some measure to depart from the practice that had hitherto obtained in this country. But now the war is over, and to my mind it is high time we got back to the observance of the rules of parliamentary Government that have obtained not only in the Mother Country but in all the Dominions, and which have proved to be the only foundation of democratic government.
I regret to say, Mr. Speaker, that the departure which has been made in this country is most pronounced in connection 9
with the office of Prime Minister. Most of all the Prime Minister must be the actual leader of his Government, and he must lead one at least of the Houses of Parliament. That has always been the practice, and I regret that owing to the illness of the Prime Minister he has not been able to lead this House for many months, and there is not much prospect that we will soon return to the old practice. On behalf of the people of this country, irrespective of any party, I say that it is time we discussed for a moment what constitutes parliamentary government, to see if it is not in the interests of the country to come back to it, and particularly to come back to it in connection with the office of the Prime Minister.
Not only must the Prime Minister lead the House and the Government, but he is also responsible for something else:	He
must select the ministers of his Government, and he must see that those ministers are elected. We have reached a hiatus when that is not taking place, and the responsibility is on the Unionist Party-the party that won the war and has a very creditable record to its account. Therefore as a friend of Union Government and as one who has supported 'every proposal made by that Government in this House to win the war, I shall call attention to what I think ought to be done to recover our position.
The main thing I wish to call attention to is that we must come back to the old practice. I regret that the Prime Minister is away. I regret that he saw fit to offer to resign his position because of overstrain due to his strenuous labours of the past few years, and he has my fullest sympathy. But the government of the country must go on, and the Unionist Party must vindicate its position and carry on the government of this country on established lines or something will happen.
Now, what is to be done? I am waiting to hear from ministers of the Union Government to tell us what they propose to do.
They do not know.

I am waiting to
hear when they intend to resume parliamentary responsibility and to have a Prime Minister in the House who leads the Government, who selects his ministers, who sees that those ministers are elected, and who can make an appeal to our fellow-countrymen who live in the province of Quebec. There never was a period in the history of this country heretofore when that appeal was not made and the Government of the



day was not able to get support from the province of Quebec and also from some of the western provinces. It may be all very well to trifle with this question and attempt to "put it over" and to suggest this and that artifice, but in doing that you get away from the question of responsible Government. Let us come back to responsible Government; and will the House bear with me when I say this: That I am making no personal comment or criticism on the right hon gentleman who has led the House so successfully as head of the Government, and who has made a great place for himself in the history of the conduct of this war. But the King's Government must go on, and it must do so under Parliamentary rules and practice. We are getting away from that. The Prime Minister is not here, and he has not done what the Unionist party have been promising for two years now, ever since they came into office. When they first had Union Government formed, we were promised that later on there would be a reconstruction of the Government. Why is that reconstruction not going on? There is some reason for that, and probably it is owing to the absence of the Prime Minister. If that be the case, I say that the responsibility is. on this Union Government to correct what is wrong and to try to return to that responsible Government that we have had in this country in the past, but that we do not happen to have at the present moment as we ought, especially now that the war is over. The people want responsible Government. I have been out in the country; I have met the people; I have read the newspapers; I have heard discussions at various public meetings. I saw what took place in Ontario recently when there was an absence of responsible Government there, when not even a caucus of a party was called to see what sort of a policy the Conservative party would have in the provincial election that took place there. And what happened? That party disappeared in a night, because it had failed to call together its friends and the people of Ontario in general to discuss the welfare of the country and the programme under which it proposed to appeal to the people. The same thing may happen in the case of the Dominion if we do not come back to Parliamentary practice and if we do not have in this House a responsible Prime Minister leading the House, forming his Government, having his Government elected, and seeing that all the country is fairly represented in the administration that attempts to carry on the affairs of the country.

There are many other questions that I should like to bring up on this occasion. I should like to discuss the question of public ownership of railways. I should like to discuss our future relations with the Empire. I should like to discuss what I know or rather what I do not know about the commitments that have been made in connection with the Imperial Conferences that have been held in the old land. We, the people of Canada, do not know what has taken place there; we do not know what commitments have been made in connection with those conferences, and we have not our Prime Minister here to tell us what took place at those conferences although he was one of the chief actors at them. While the war was a great success, I should like to know whether we shared in the proper responsibility of that war, and I should also like to know something about our position in the League of Nations.
I hope to be able to discuss that later on I should like to discuss the fiscal policy of this country. I have heard a good deal about it here to-day, and I heard the hon. member for Lethbridge ,(Mr. Buchanan) and another hon. member speak about a measure of redistribution that should take place next year. I do not want to see an election in this country until that measure of redistribution has been put through this House; but when it has been put through, I want to see representation by population as the groundwork principle in that redistribution. We have not had it. I represent in this House about 100,000 people; some time ago, I represented many more than that, and my constituency is growing rapidly. We ought to have in this House three votes from that constituency in settling the policy of the country and in maintaining Parliamentary and democratic institutions in Canada. You cannot have democratic institutions in this country unless you have representation by population. The United States have that, if it exists anywhere. We must have it here, and I want to appeal especially to my friends from the West who were saying here to-day, and justly saying, that there should be full representation from the West in this House before we have an election. I want to see full representation for every section of the country, for Quebec, for Ontario, as well as for the West. I bring this up merely because I desire to say that that is another topic that I should like to discuss in this House, but I am going to leave all those questions for another opportunity. The debate is not over; and while it has wandered

far afield, and while the leader of the Opposition has asked for an election, a proposition which I cannot see my way to accept, what I want to see is a return to responsible Parliamentary Government, no matter who makes the sacrifice in order that it may come back. Especially do I appeal to the members of the Government and to its supporters to see that we come back to a condition of affairs where the Prime Minister is in the country at the head of the Government, where he is reconstructing the Government as he promised to do and as the people expect him to do. I say this all the time remembering that he is ill, but nevertheless, the Government must go on. In all fairness and in the most respectful way I direct the attention of the Government of the daj/ and my fellow members of the House, especially those who have supported Union Government, to try to come back to the principle of responsible Government and to show that the Unionist party is able to strengthen itself, to select ministers, to elect them in the country, and to put forward a policy necesary for reconstruction. If we do not do that-and I <am going to speak very plainly, and I think I can see what is going on-we shall have cabals in the ministry instead of leadership, instead of a progressive, policy. Every one can see signs of these things. Unfortunately, those who wish to depart from the observance and maintenance of responsible Parliamentary Government in this country seem to be ministers of the Grown.
I hope the ministers of the Crown will realize their double responsibility and come back to responsible Parliamentary Government, and have the Government reconstructed. Let us have a Prime Minister in his place who will assume responsibility and lead the House and the country in thi3 great duty of reconstruction.
Does my hon. friend suggest that the Prime Minister should resign?

I do not make
any suggestion at the moment. I say that the Prime Minister wished to resign and did resign, and probably that is his disposition now, but apparently some of his friends wish to keep him in an irresponsible position.

Seeing
that the hon. member has attacked the Prime Minister, would he be good enough to say whether he has attended one-fifth as many sittings of this House as the 91
Prime Minister during the last five years, during which he has been drawing his full indemnity?

I have not attacked the Prime Minister. I have the greatest respect for him. Many a time has he asked my advice, and I have been pleased to give it to him. Many a time I have spoken on the platform with him in constituencies and helped him to elect his candidates. I have not always been in this ' House as much as I should have been, but I have been in this House a good deal, and whenever I have spoken it has been on a real question. I am speaking on a real question to-day, one that is uppermost in the minds of the people of this country, and uppermost in the minds of the ministry, many of whom are anxious to lead a way out of the situation. I am not calling for the Prime Minister's resignation. I am calling for the observance of the principle of responsible parliamentary government. I have heard a good deal around this House and have seen a great deal in the newspapers about this very question. I saw it in the Montreal papers, for instance.

Might I ask my hon. friend whether he was in his seat to-day and heard the statement of the leader of the Government (Sir George Foster) in reference to the absence of the Prime Minister, and if so, whether he approves of the statement that was made?
I heard the statement.
What objections have you to it?

The objections
will be removed when we return to responsible parliamentary government. That is all I want. We have not had responsible parliamentary government in this country, I must tell the hon. gentleman.
, What do you suggest should be done?

I am calling attention to the situation. Perhaps we shall have a further discussion of it. I am discussing a real question, and I believe I am speaking for the people of Canada today. I am passing no reflections wftatso-ever on the right hon. gentleman who leads the House. I am simply trying to speak for the people of this country on a matter

of paramount importance to them. The disturbance following the war is great, the dislocations are many, and all sorts of new conditions have come into existence. One underlying principle of our constitution is that of responsible parliamentary government, and I say that we have got some way away from that in this House. During the war the country was ruled by Orders in Council, and very properly so perhaps; other nations had to do it, but now we should return to responsible government and get on with a policy of reconstruction. There is many a minister in the Government to-day who I would like to see giving most of his time to framing policies of reconstruction to lay before the House. Any such measures will have any little support I may be able to give them. Again I say, I arose in my place here today to ask that the Unionist Government come back at the very earliest possible moment to responsible parliamentary government and bring forward the necessary legislation for the reconstruction of the country. I do not think theie should be an election, if it can be avoided, until there has been a numbering of the people. That could begin on the first of April next year and be completed thirty days thereafter and a report made, on which a redistribution measure could be based and introduced in the following May, then with a new Franchise Act and a new Redistribution measure, let there be an appeal to the people in a general election.
Mr. H. A. FORTIER (Labeile). (translation) : We are meeting this year in our new Parliament Building which adorns the historic hill of the Capital, resplendent like a gothic marvel of old. Fifty years ago, Mr. Speaker, the representatives of the Canadian people were meeting here for the first time after Confederation.
On that occasion, the representatives of the people came from all the provinces and there were on the ministerial benches the two minsters representing the two great races in this country. Those ministers had joined their efforts to make Canada a great country, a united and prosperous country. They gave the first administration we had in this Dominion the name of Macdonald-Cartier, a name never to be forgotten. If I recall this happening of bygone days, it is to show by what spirit the Fathers of Confederation were prompted and. at the same time, to underline the present policy of the Unionist party, which has become occasionally the successor of the former

Governments, of the Macdonald-Cartier Government, and which is, nevertheless, driving the country to disunion and to ruin.
In 1867, we, in the province of Quebec, were associated with the English provinces of 'Canada and put on an equal footing with them by a federative compact assented to by the 'Imperial Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. In this agreement the rights of the first pioneers, the rights of my ancestors were preserved; they could say that the survival of all their rights, customs and traditions was secured by this Act.
When the negotiations previous to Confederation took place, Macdonald was not in favour of a Federative Act, he would Rave preferred a Legislative union; but Cartier, whose opinion finally prevailed, wished the provinces to retain their full autonomy, while Canada would be ruled by a central federal power. The first meeting wjhich took place under the Confederation Act carried with itself a meaning far different from and far more eloquent than that of our present meeting. In 1867, both races *were represented in the Cabinet, which took pleasure in asserting this dual character to the extent of styling itself the Macdonald-Cartier administration. Therefore though the House of Commons of 1867 was smaller than that of 1920, it embraced more, because it was taking in, amid the cheers of the people, a ministry, it was taking in members who came from all the provinces and by whom all nationalities were represented. On that occasion, Cartier might well say to the Dominion, as he did " For more than a century, the British flag, which bears the name of Union, has unfurled its folds on the horizon of Canada. That century, now elapsed, was rather marked by quarrels between the two races which are going to constitute a new people, the Canadian people. That protracted strife has known hours of conflict more cruel than others, but the secular contact between the two races seems to have finally resulted in creating a better conception of their respective worth and, as a sequence, a new spirit, born of a friendly understanding which prevails at last. In time, we shall have a country where there is neither victor nor vanquished, neither a superior nor an inferior race. We have Confederation accepted at last by the Mother Country and by the colony. Confederation will give us a Canadian country, a country which will be really united, for on the occasion of an event of this kind, the union of the minds cannot be but a word, an empty word, it

carries with itself a cordiality which will make a people endowed with the gifts of the two most glorious nations of the world and, therefore, a people which, young though it be as yet, will undertake, in a masterly way, to carry out its destinies."
On the other hand, Macdonald withstood, in the full measure of his might, the brunt of the attacks of the few British statesmen, more enthusiastic than clearsighted, who required the help of the colony in the wars of England with the nations of the world, his answer being that Canada was under no obligation to contribute money or men to enterprises with respect to which she had no say. How far we are, Mr. Speaker, from the spirit of those leaders all engrossed by the problems of Canadian politics and devoting the whole of their intelligence and the very best of their heart to the realization of the ideal which had inspired the Fathers of Confederation:	"Make Canada
- a united, happy and prosperous country." The policy of the Government, as expressed in the speech from the Throne, deals hut with external affairs, matters concerning the world at large, which may offer some interest to the Allies now that the peace treaty has been signed, which may have a direct interest for London, Paris or Washington, for instance, hut those questions are of such a nature as to have us, citizens of this country, perfectly indifferent. It might perhaps be interesting to hear it mentioned in the speech from the throne, among the great deeds of the Government, that a commercial treaty has been signed with the most powerful nations; but what is to us the signature of a peace treaty with Bulgaria or with Turkey? Have we ever declared war to those far distant countries? And was war ever declared to us by those countries?
I am sure the Government do not think we are gullible enough to believe them when they say that we should be glad of these signatures being there because they mean a diplomatic success for an ambassador of the Canadian nation. Has not the Government anything besides matters of foreign policy of which they could assume the merit in the Speech from the Throne? Have we become, perchance, an independent state? I should be glad of it, for it means the crowning of a people's legitimate aspirations toward complete autonomy and freedom. But nobody here spoke of breaking our colonial bonds and so far Great Britain has not notified us that starting from a certain date, say from the coming into power of the Union Government for instance, we should become an independent and free country, not a sister nation, hut an absolutely independent and self-governing nation. *	'
Fortunately we know by experience what a speech from the Throne means for a Government. It is an official document in which no mention is made of the questionable legislation which the Government in-tendg enacting-as evidenced at the last session when they brought up at the last minute the monster bill for the acquisition of the Grand Trunk

but which gives the Government credit- for foreign legislation to which they never contributed, or expresses delight at the occurring of events which we may look upon with indifference but which however are a disguise for the shameful sacrificing of our autonomy to imperialism.
Imperialism, Mr. Speaker, is the enemy. It is on account of imperialism that our national debt reached the enormous figure of $2,000,000,000 and that nothing seems to be able to stop its rise which is leading this country to disaster. It is also on account of imperialism that our expenses, including the cost of administration, the large sum of interest on our loans and the necessary funds for the soldiers' pensions, are continuously widening the abyss of our indebtedness which taxation is unable'to fill. That is not all the harm that Imperialism will cause this country. It is bound to lead us to militarism.
The League of Nations finds it impossible to control the war-like preparations of the Allies. The Great Powers have never been so anxious to keep up and to increase their military force than -since the signing of peace: Great Britain and the United States, their navy; France, her army.
What is the secret mission on . which the representative of the British navy, Lord Jellicoe, was sent to this Government? What new contribution did the Government pledge to Lord Jellicoe? There is nothing in the speech from the Throne about it and the acting leader of the Government remains silent on the matter. But deeds are more eloquent than words. The very warm and cordial reception given to the admiral- thanks to which our Prime Minister was taken aboard the flagship to be carried away to other colonies of the Empire as a living mark of our subjection-the silence observed by the Government and the coinminatory stand taken by its leader, are so many facts which are much more telling than any speech from the Throne could be.
Canada is being threatened now more than ever by this dangerous policy and

active form of imperialism which will hind our future welfare, our resources and our children to satisfy the ambition of a country devoted to militarism. [DOT]
I am happy to be a member of the political association which,, at its last session, held in Ottawa last summer, did not hesitate to adopt as an important plank of its platform: That the constitution of Canada shall not in any way be modified as regards our relationship to Great Britain, without the people being previously consulted.
We, the descendants of the discoverers and pioneers of this country, as well as the newcomers who wish to make of this fertile land their home, were not entrusted by Providence with the task of perpetuating on this American continent the causes of conflicts which are keeping the old European countries continuously afire, but we were asked to devote our efforts to the beneficent works of. peace, to work with a legitimate emulation for the development of our immense resources and to establish here a free, contented and prosperous country.
There is another question which though it does not appear in the speech from the Throne, hovers however in the mind of the Government. I am referring to divorce. At a previous session, the Government had already overlooked an attempt to introduce a bill to make divorce easier. Owing to persistent rumors which have been circulating even in this Parliament, there is some apprehension that the Government will favour such anti-christian legislation.
The country is bound to suffer from such a law jf it be adopted by this Parliament. Divorce is the greatest menace to the maintenance of family ties, and the family is the basic social institution.
At this dangerous period where revolutions are about to break out, where the spirit of bolshevism penetrates and spreads almost everywhere, and where strife between classes, animated by passions which are a menace to public order, voiced even in this Parliament, it is time that we should prepare to safeguard the interests of society and see that they are preserved from the scourge of divorce. Christian minds and orderly people understand that such legislation would be most dangerous. Are we not,, then, in a Christian country? The Fathers of Confederation themselves had foreseen the disastrous consequences which society would derive from a law by which divorce had been made easy. They have shown toleration for it, but at the same time they have rendered it as difficult as

possible at every turn, surrounding the proceedings with all kinds of precautions and intrusting the responsibility of the decree solely to that honourable and revered body which personifies the wisdom of the nation. Such toleration by the constitution may lead to' abuse. I would suggest that the British North America Act be amended so as to make divorce an impossibility, in this country.
The Government prides itself of its recent participation in the first international labour congress. If it be an honour for the Government to send representatives to a conference of that kind, *where they will meet the spokesmen of capital and of labour, let us wish that this participation may procure such amount of experience as is necessary to solve the anguishing problem of labour in this country.
But who will supply the generating principle of happy solutions in social life? I have the honour to belong to that class of men who believe that this problem can be solved only in the light of Christian principles. Such solutions, obtained through a recourse to the great principle of social truth,, with which the 'Church is possessed, are yet the most durable and the most practical. The revered leaders of our church have had very much at heart, for a long time, the happiness of the workingmen, of all the men who toil; but one of them has dealt with the social question, in our age, with more striking effect than the others. His authority was recognized by all the statesmen and his advice was followed, and happily so,, in many countries. The great Pope Leo XIII, surnamed the workingmen's Pope, gave the universe the encyclical letter " Berum novarum ", The document was greeted in all the industrial cities, as the charter of the social world, that is, as a full treatise on that subject,, as a symposium of the reforms which the working classes of the world have the right to seek for the betterment of their condition and the welfare of their families as well. It is in the light of those two principles so marvelously just and true, that so many national and catholic trade unions were organized in our province of Quebec. Whenever those associations have sought to assert themselves publicly among the working classes of Canada, they have invariably been spurned by this Government.
I pray this Government, as I would particularly pray the hon. minister of Labour if he had a seat in this House, to give a just attention to the legitimate claims

of those bodies of workingmen in my province. You will perhaps find, in the useful work which they have already accomplished, some guiding principles which may help you in your future legislation with respect to labour.
Now, Mr. Speaker, much has been said .about a particular item of the speech from the Throne relating to a new Franchise Act,' which leads us to discuss the opportunity of a new general election in this country.	[DOT]
I was amused, a moment ago, to hear the reflections made by some hon. members on the other side of the House. They would have us believe that they have no fear of the electorate, but they lay down as a principle that we should differ, as long as possible, to consult the people. I think that is a false principle and that it is impossible to wait till the next census has been taken, before we have a general election in this country. The last census was taken in 1911 and the next one will be taken in 1921. That does not mean that the election may be arranged in such a way as to satisfy the claims expressed by the members from the Canadian West and take place during the year 1921, because the delays necessary to complete the work must be taken into account, and therefore, a general election could not be held before the year 1923. What is just and what the people is expecting is that a general election should take place as soon as possible. There seems to be a unanimous chorus of protests not only on this side of the House, but on the other side as well, to the effect that the affairs of the country should be administered by another government.
Quite often and how emphatically have we been told that the present Government was returned in 1917 for the period of the war, that this was a Government formed so as to win the rvar and styled a Union Government.
Now that war is over and peace is signed, that we enter upon an era of reconstruction, the citizen of Canada are bound to call upon their leaders to lay their policy before them so that they may choose their representatives. The present Government is inclined to wait until the next census before holding general elections. General elections woud be as fair now as in 1923. The people might avail themselves of their privileges during 1920 and again during 1923; they would be at liberty to choose their representatives and their rulers.
As for us, we can see no reason for the delaying of the elections on the part of the Administration.
In the province which it is my privilege to inhabit, where we are under the rule of a Liberal Government, they do not wait, like the Conservatives and the Tories, until the end of a parliament to hold new elections ; they know how to respect the rights and bow to the will of the people, every three years, or every four years at the utmost. The Union Government should follow such an example; and we on this side of the House would be only too willing that general elections should be held as soon as possible.
The old walls of the first parliamentary buildings of Confederation had witnessed many events redounding to the glory of our Canadian statesmen. Indeed, within those walls flourished such men as Cartier, Macdonald, Mackenzie, Mowat, Chapleau and Laurier, and many others, and I must be content with mentioning only those who have departed, omitting the men who are still in active life on either side of this House. It is no part of these remarks to extol what they have done. But let us feelingly. remember them and hail their patriotism.
The last and greatest of that line of illustrious men used to say: "The twentieth century will be the century of Canada." Like him, let us have faith in the future of this country. Let the new walls of these precincts forever bear through ages the stamp of events which shall conduce to the greatness and success of our common country.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) this afternoon, you will have noticed, mixed with his tears and lamentations on the loss of responsible and representative government and the decay of democracy several earnest expressions of hope, together with the utterance of jl desire to speak on this, that and the other subject and to deal with matters of various descriptions. The trouble with the hon. member for South York, who, as every one knows, is possessed of a very fertile brain, is that he does not attend the House often enough to have an opportunity to give expression to these excellent ideas of his.

\
Consequently they accumulate and become an incubus upon the hon. gentleman. We are all, I am sure, in perfect sympathy with that hon. member in his expressions of opinion with regard to representative government. These are good words; they have a pleasant sound. The word " democracy " also, which unfortunately is often misused and sometimes much abused, nevertheless is equally well-sounding, and no person can use it with greater unction and force than the hon. member for South York. It is true that Cabinet ministers, by virtue of the position they occupy, are clothed with special responsibilities; but it is likewise true that members of Parliament who are elected to represent the people in the House of Commons have also certain responsibilities to their constituencies, one of which responsibilities-a most important - one- is that they shall be as regular as possible in their attendance and shall give as much time as they can to the business of the country. I say this, Mr. Speaker, merely because I think that possibly a criticism of the absence of the Prime Minister or of any other Cabinet minister would come with rather better grace from any other hon. gentleman in this House than the hon. member for South York. I have listened, as I am sure all hon. gentlemen have listened, with a great deal of pleasure and interest to the speeches delivered by the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton, N.B., (Mr. Caldwell), and by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould). I hope I shall not be misunderstood when I say that I think that the hon. gentleman who represents the constituency in New Brunswick is a vast improvement on his predecessor. I do not by any means want him to rest complacently under such an impression.
Now, Sir, in the speech of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie JCing) the other day, that hon. gentleman bewailed

the fact that there had been some delay in calling on elections, and he waxed eloquent in referring to the lapse of time between the occurrence of the vacancy and the calling of the election to fill it. Now, the remedy lay in the hands of the Laurier Government, of which my hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) was a distinguished -and shining light even at that time, and it probably did not occur to the hon. gentleman that he might with propriety direct some of his remarks to some of those whose -seats would be near him if they were in the House. This, however, is something which does not seem to occur to the hon. gentleman -as calling for so-me attention on his part. But the -hon. gentleman in that statement was exhibiting a modesty of which I really did not think him capable. He might have -said that a by-election was also extremely useful to the leader of -an opposition in indicating the same thing. Perhaps he will allow me to- remind him that there was -a by-election out in Assiniboia. We had -a -most eloquent speech this afternoon -from the representative of that constituency (Mr. Gould), who bears a very attractive name. But apparently, in

Now, the speech from the Throne tells us that peace has been concluded with Bulgaria and that the Treaty ratifying that peace will presently he submitted - to this House for its consideration. The fact that Canada has found herself in the position of making a Treaty of Peace with Bulgaria carries a great significence with it, and brings home at once to one's mind the place our country occupies to-day among the nations of the world. We have heard ,a good deal from ministers of the Crown in regard to the altered position which Canada now occupies as a result of our participation in the war, and particularly of our participation in the making of peace. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Howell), who, I regret, is not in his seat, has told us- and it has also been told us by some of his colleagues-that 'Canada has attained the full status of a nation, that we have grown away from the position which we occupied in the past. My attention was attracted a few weeks ago by an address delivered by the President of the Privy Council in the city of Ottawa, in the course of which he took strong exception to certain resolutions that were about to be brought before the American Senate dealing with Canada's relations to the League of Nations. Now, there is to my mind a distinction here, and One can understand the position that some

of our American cousins take upon this question, and I would offer the suggestion to- the Government that they should walk circumspectly in regard to it. After all, this question of Canada's status as a nation has yet to be determined.
We were told by the hon. the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell), in his speech on the Peace Treaty last autumn, that Canada had acquired a new status, that every one recognized it and that at the forthcoming Imperial Conference which was-to be held this summer he felt quite sure that the steps would be taken to accord Canada that position. If that is to be done I think it is a question that should -be discussed by this Parliament before it is settled by any members of the Government which may attend an Imperial Conference. No matter what these changes may involve, they are too momentous, too far-reaching in their possibilities to be delegated to a small group from our Government, no matter how able or conscientious these representatives may be, Consequently, I for one, take the position that if the Government have in contemplation anything which they propose to place before the Imperial Conference in this regard they should bring it before the House and get an expression of opinion from Parliament before Canada is committed to any particular line of action in respect to it.

Now, in what field of development can we most readily and easily find a response in this country? I submit, Sir, that it is in agriculture; and I venture this statement, that if Canada in the last forty years had given one quarter of the assistance in the development of agriculture that she has accorded directly by way of bounties and indirectly by way of a protective tariff, to manufacturing industries in the Dominion, our wealth as a nation would be greater and our population would be larger than it is at the present time. I would point out to the House the excellent and splendid advantage that Canada enjoys in this regard. We have a country that is essentially an agricultural country. We know that our provinces, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, are rich in agricultural possibilities. We can take the Maritime Provinces, and we can take the province of Quebec and the province of Ontario; they contain vast undeveloped agricultural possibilities. We have our Western ,prairies that are as capable of producing one billion bushels of wheat as they are of producing three hundred million bushels. Finally we have the province of British Columbia where resources, although more varied, still contain great agricultural possibilities. I would direct this thought again to my protectionist friends in this House, that the farmers of this country are to-day in the position, where they are selling practically everything they produce in open competition with the world and are buying in a restricted market everything they require for the purpose of production. I can say also that it will take a very long time indeed to convince the farmers of western Canada, for example, that there is any virtue in the principle of protection, especially in a customs tariff. The argument of the protectionist is that we must have this form of state assistance to industry in order to build up a home market and make us independent of outside countries.
But the fact is that we would require 50,000,000 souls- to consume the wheat we now produce in this country, and the same applies to practically every other line of our agricultural products. Let us look at the opportunities that lie ahead of us. Canada occupies the northern half of this continent. Immediately to the south of us. there is a vast country that will soon become a food importing country. To-day

the population of the United States probably reaches 112,000,000 to 115,000,000 souls; within fifteen or twenty years that population may reach 140,000,000. To-day they are within measurable distance of becoming a food importing nation-indeed, in some respects they are now importing the food stuffs we produce.
They have a surplus of everything the farmer has to sell, and we have not.	*

They are reaching the
point, I say, when they will be a food importing nation. We have also the excellent advantage of our relationship with the British market, which is a great consuming market. Where does the Britisher get the greater part of the food he eats-the meats and the wheat, and the coarse grains that he requires for his live stock? He has to buy them in-the outside markets of the world. When he buys from the Argentine Republic he has to haul his purchases twice the distance that he requires to carry them from Canada; if he buys in Australia he has to haul them three times the distance, and if he buys in India the haul is more than double that from this country. Consequently, I pay again, Canada as an agricultural country occupies a unique and splendid place in the world to-day. And it does seem to me, Mr. Speaker,-and I have never stated anything with more sincerity than I state this to-night-that it is the part of very great wisdom that we in future direct our energies to the development of our agricultural resources, and in fact to the development ol our natural resources of all kinds. .

We have large areas that could well be reforested. These bounties of nature will not last forever, and it is the part of wisdom now to lay the foundation for maintaining the supplies of these resources that are necessary for human happiness and human progress.

He referred to the Agrarian Movement, and he associated with that the idea of class legislation and class domination. I take issue with my hon. friend in that regard. He has been a Protectionist all his life, he has believed in that principle during the many years it has dominated the fiscal polity of this country, and yet I maintain that there never was perpetrated upon this country a greater instance of class legislation than is to be found in the operation of that principle. What is the purpose of a tariff? It is designed to benefit a particular section of the people, it operates in no other way, and consequently the operation of this protective system in our fiscal policy, which has obtained largely for the last forty years, has conferred upon a special class a privilege that in my judgment is not compatible with a true democracy. And I would point out to my hon. friend from Brantford and to other hon. gentlemen also who believe in a protective tariff, that Protection is nothing more or less than a type of State Socialism. It is State assistance to particular industries, and just as surely as night follows day it will bring this development in its train. If you have a protective tariff you must have your boards of commerce and your regulative bodies that will endeavour to control the thing that you have built up. It was true in Germany, and it was true in the United States, for they were inevitably coming to it if they had not largely modified their fiscal system some seven or eight years ago.

Mr. Speaker, the question has also been asked: Where will the revenue come from if we do away with the protective tariff? In that respect I have just this to say, that I am not at all sure that we would not get more revenue, for instance, out of woollen duties if they were on a basis of fifteen per cent than when they are on a basis of thirty per cent. But the Agrarians-and I thank my honourable friend from Brantford for coining that title for me-do not wish to sweep away the tariff at one fell blow ais some people are trying to make out; that is not their policy. Broadly speaking, their policy is based on the principle that the implements and tools of production should be free and that the necessaries of life should be made as free as possible, and in that regard they asked for a substantial all-round reduction in the customs tariff. A tariff on luxuries? Yes, keep it on and raise it higher, but I cannot see the exact wisdom of having certain classes of luxuries imported into this country as they are to-day at a lower rate of duty than that imposed on necessities of life such as cotton, boots and shoes. I would offer this suggestion to the Minister of Finance that he might well raise the tax on luxuries to 50 per cent if he likes; but when he does that, he should also impose an excise tax on the manufacturer in Canada of such luxuries.
But those who have been called the agrarians have certain concrete proposals in respect to revenue. We have the -income tax, and the income tax has come to stay
in this country. I find from the statistics that .for the years 1915 to 1918, the little country of New Zealand collected in income tax over $55,000,000. The population of New Zealand, based on its census of 1916, is roughly 1,100,000. I would suggest this as a fertile field to explore in respect of securing revenue.
We are told that if we raise our income taxes, all the wealthy people, who enjoy large incomes will cross the border, and that consequently that source of income would -be shut off from us. What do we find in the United -States? In the year 1919, for instance, the United States collected in income and excess profits taxes over $2,600,000,000. If Canada had collected at the same ratio according to population we would have collected over $200,000,000. I know the difficulty of organizing a system of income taxation. But I will point -this out, that in New Zealand and Australia these income taxes were, -I believe, practically in all cases assessed after the outbreak of war. In these countries, British -countries like our own, they have perfected their machinery at any rate to the point where they are getting vastly more for their revenue -than we are in Canada.
